claims.claim: The 'march of progress' image (Rudolph Zallinger, 'The Road to Homo Sapiens', Time-Life 'Early Man', 1965) became a much-copied and parodied icon
sources: Cosmos Magazine: Evolution of an icon
Yale Alumni Magazine: March of progress
claims.note: Image NOT reproduced (copyright); film shows our own pictogram of the popular idea, labelled

claims.claim: Ernst Haeckel drew a 'Pedigree of Man' tree with Man at the top, published 1874 (Anthropogenie / The Evolution of Man)
sources: Wikimedia Commons: Pedigree of man (Haeckel 1874).jpg (public domain)

claims.claim: Darwin sketched a branching tree headed 'I think' in Notebook B, 1837
sources: Cambridge University Library, Darwin Notebook B p.36

claims.claim: Sahelanthropus tchadensis ('Toumai'), Chad, about 7 million years old, found 2001, may be near the human-chimpanzee split; whether it walked upright is debated
sources: Macchiarelli et al. 2020, J. Human Evolution (not convinced)

claims.claim: Laetoli footprints, Tanzania, about 3.66 million years old, show upright bipedal walking
sources: Smithsonian Human Origins: Laetoli footprint trails

claims.claim: Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) found at Hadar, Ethiopia, 1974; about 3.2 million years old; small brain (~380-550 cc), legs adapted for walking
sources: Institute of Human Origins, ASU: Lucy

claims.claim: Koobi Fora, Kenya, ~1.5 million years ago: footprints of Paranthropus boisei (12-print trail) and Homo erectus (3 prints) on the same lakeshore surface
sources: Science News: Footprints offer a rare look at ancient human relatives crossing paths
claims.note: species IDs inferred from footprint shape (authors' hypothesis)

claims.claim: Homo erectus fossils from Africa, Georgia (Dmanisi), China and Java; last known at Ngandong, Java, 117,000-108,000 years ago; species span > 1.5 million years (~1.9 Ma to ~0.11 Ma)
Jebel Irhoud, Morocco: fossils ~315,000 years old described as early Homo sapiens; some experts see them as a form on the way to modern humans
sources: Hublin et al. 2017 and Richter et al. 2017, Nature

claims.claim: Homo naledi, Rising Star cave, South Africa, dated 335,000-236,000 years ago; brain ~465-610 cc (less than half of modern ~1,350 cc)
Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia; brains as large as (on average slightly larger than) modern humans'; disappeared ~41,000-39,000 years ago
Denisovans are known mostly from DNA; first genome from a finger bone from Denisova Cave, published 2010
Homo floresiensis, Flores: about a metre tall (LB1 ~1.06 m); skeletal remains ~100,000-60,000 years old; brain ~426 cc (about chimpanzee size); stone tools at Liang Bua
sources: Kubo et al. 2013, Proc. R. Soc. B

claims.claim: Homo luzonensis, Callao Cave, Luzon, named 2019; fossils at least 50,000-67,000 years old (minimum ages, may be older)
A little over 100,000 years ago, as many as six kinds of human may have been alive at once (sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, erectus to ~108 ka, floresiensis, luzonensis)
claims.method: overlap of the date ranges above; luzonensis has only minimum ages, so 'as many as' and 'may'

claims.claim: About 2% of non-African genomes come from Neanderthals (estimates ~1.5-4%); some Papua New Guinea populations carry several percent Denisovan DNA (estimates up to ~5%, varying by method)
Stephen Jay Gould criticised the march-of-progress image in Wonderful Life (1989), chapter 'The Iconography of an Expectation'
claims.note: on screen as a paraphrase, not a direct quote
